utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case but not until after I've wished a good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I notice, Mr. Stewart, that Ms. Loukas isn't there at this moment. Do you expect her to arrive or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think she's working on 92 bis at the moment, and she will be along later this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, then. Yesterday I indicated to the parties that I would allow them just to make some brief additional remarks this morning. Is there -- on the issue of the presentation of 92 bis material in respect of the witness Babic, especially -- and I think I'm very much focused on the 1.100 pages of the Milosevic trial material. Is there any need to make any further observations? Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a great deal to add. I would respectfully suggest that we consider taking the opportunity presented by the meeting this afternoon at 2.30 to address the mechanics in a more collaborative manner. I simply want to stress that there were many steps that might have been taken to mitigate or alleviate any problems resulting from the material during -- while the motion was pending. So perhaps we could use the opportunity this afternoon to at least identify the most effective way of dealing with the issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. So you'd rather postpone further discussions to this afternoon. You'll understand that this is a -- I would say a significant procedural issue which, if possible, we would like to deal with in open court. That's one. And there's another issue, and it is that Mr. Babic better be able to -- to get to that point is a different matter, but Mr. Babic is expected to start his testimony next Tuesday, and if we would take a decision later this afternoon... So I don't know whether we're going to delay a decision until that moment, but even if we would give a decision and if there would be good reasons to just change it a bit, then we could even consider that. Mr. Stewart, would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect, we -- we do endorse Your Honour's comment about dealing with these important procedural matters in open court. Apart from the obvious reasons, there is the fact that that does enable Mr. Krajisnik to hear them, because after all, he doesn't attend the meetings that we're talking about this afternoon. The -- yes, we had, as we said we would, we have had some thoughts and I've had some discussion was my team overnight. The -- I -- as a sort of starting point, I think about the way that some of these things are sometimes dealt with in domestic proceedings. Not to say that we should just immediately translate them to here, but as a starting point. If one has some written material, say some evidence that a witness has given in previous proceedings, or has given evidence on affidavit and you want to introduce into this particular trial the same material, now, one way of doing it, if it's a short passage, is to ask the witness to look at that passage and confirm that that is what he would say to this and will say to this particular Trial Chamber. That has the advantage, which I think is an advantage in a way, that it actually sidesteps the 92 bis procedure altogether, as we see it, because then it effectively becomes that witness's direct evidence - direct in the broad sense - in this particular case. There is, however, a real practical problem with that before this Tribunal, which is that it's only really available in relation to very short bits of evidence, because there is this practical problem which we are facing, that these transcripts - and we're often talking about transcripts, of course - they're not available in B/C/S, so that Mr. Babic as the witness -- because we'd thought to ourselves, well, could he be given selected bits in advance, but he can't because they're not available in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stewart, if I may interrupt you. There would be a solution for that, that he could listen, at least, to the original testimony by using the B/C/S tape of the Milosevic trial. I think that would be a solution. Mr. Tieger, I see you are raising your eyebrows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I stay on my feet on this one, Your Honour, because, rather than to'ing and fro'ing -- I'm not wishing to stifle Mr. Tieger or the Tribunal, but I think it might be better to deal with it that way, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We thought about that as well, Your Honour. The real difficulty with that - and we're not Mr. Babic's counsel, but for anybody trying to do that - first of all, it's a minor problem. We know from practical experience from our own client that these tapes are extremely unreliable. That's point number 1. They really are very difficult to handle and are extremely unreliable in practice. But that's a subsidiary point. It's -- it's pretty difficult, and it's very time-consuming for anybody, certainly it's impossible for Mr. Krajisnik to deal with it given the volume of material, but even for a witness of Mr. Babic's position in relation to any significant quantity of material, dealing with it on the audiotape is really, we suggest, not a practical option. It's far too onus, it's far too unwieldy, it's far too difficult for somebody to handle. In relation to very short passages, there isn't a problem because in relation to short passages of just a few paragraphs at the most, or 20 lines, of course counsel can read those out, they can be translated, the witness can hear them, they can be confirmed. It is still quicker than inviting the witness to go over the same ground again by question and answer. As long as it's -- the passage doesn't involve anything which is objectionably leading so that we would -- for example, in relation to Mr. Babic we would be unhappy just to have that spoon fed to him and have him confirm it, but everybody relies on professional judgement in relation to those matters as we go alone. That works, we'd suggest, satisfactorily in relation to reasonable sized chunks of evidence. When we get to bigger chunks of evidence, perhaps there's 20 pages or something like that, with -- with sufficient notice, and that's obviously a problem in relation to Mr. Babic, with sufficient notice we'd suggest that there -- if we're talking about a very important bit of evidence that might -- but it might take quite awhile to bring out in oral evidence in chief but could be dealt with pretty quickly if the witness were able to confirm what's in that bit of transcript, that might be worth translating. It may be that the costs and the time taken in relation to the key bits -- not so key that they have to be brought out in evidence in chief orally but, if you like, key at the next level; they're important enough and specific enough to be deduced in evidence but they will be much quicker to deal with this way, it may be that the burden and the time is better transferred to the translators which, after all, is one person rather than about 20 people sitting in court while we go through it. I'm just thinking of a proper balance of resources. So far as material can't be dealt with in any of those ways, well, then I suggest we're simply driven back to what we might call conventional 92 bis. When we get to conventional 92 bis, I would simply would comment at this point, Your Honour, that we note what Your Honour said yesterday, that it took the Tribunal some time - which we understand to be slightly euphemistic - it took the Tribunal some time to have at least a global look at the material. Now, I indicated the robust approach we had to take into relation to Mr. Babic's material, but I hope Your Honour will see that that's not a satisfactory approach for the Defence to have to adopt generally in relation to 92 bis material, and we haven't. And I hope that the Tribunal having -- the Tribunal has got plenty of experience, of course, but having had the experience in relation to the volume of material and dealing with Mr. Babic's 92 bis material will begin to get perhaps a clearer idea of what is facing the Defence in dealing with 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, that's the depending issue, I would say, which is anyhow you need more time to prepare, and I can imagine that you find it a nice coincidence that the Chamber is experiencing, at least that's how you present it, similar problems as you have. Let's not -- I mean, that's sufficiently clear what your position is, with respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right, we do in a sense -- and I don't mean this cheekily if I say welcome to the real world, Your Honours, this is what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't mean offensively to suggest the Tribunal is not operating in the real world. Your Honour knows what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise, I would have made a short comment on that, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. May I make one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To meet again, both being in the real world, I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you'd like -- you'd rather not miss any opportunity to strengthen your position, and you've done that. It's clear to us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's my job, Your Honour. May I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to say to you that that message, at least, perhaps not to the depth you'd like, it's to be understood by the Chamber, but at least that you tried again, that's clear now. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say the Prosecution are big boys, and women as well, Your Honour, and can look after themselves, but we see from our side of the court how very difficult it is for a suggestion of this nature, whatever its merits for the future, to be adopted at this point in time in relation to next week. We could -- we can see that from where we sit and I'm sure the Tribunal will have that in mind. I'm sure Mr. Tiger has that in mind himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other comment to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour. I appreciate the fact that we seem to have come to a kind of sea change in the perception of 92 bis. I simply want to speak in support of what I understood to be the original underlying purpose of 92 bis, and that was to enable this institution to utilise the previous cases to incorporate, in particular, large bodies of material that had been dealt with in other cases in a way that didn't consume undue court time. Now, as I say, I appreciate that we've come to understand that it's -- it may be a double-edged sword, but I mention that because that's the basis on which we proceeded. I note that a number of the solutions, or proposed solutions, discussed this morning simply require a great deal of time and creativity. They could have been implemented before. They would be extremely difficult to implement now. I -- the Court noted the -- that Mr. Babic is expected to be on the stand soon. Nobody appreciates that fact more than me, and I simply wanted to make it clear that, in light of that, the options are limited at this point, the options of now dealing with this material in a way other than the conventional 92 bis. That was why I suggested that we take the opportunity to have a bit more collaborative discussion about the best way of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to the Chamber, Mr. Tieger. Thank you for your observations. I think we can now continue to hear the testimony of Mr. Kirudja. Madam Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just say I wonder at what point it would be convenient for Your Honours to deal with the issue which is still on the table in relation to that correspondence to Mr. Harmon and Mrs. Del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I went through the correspondence again yesterday. I also checked what the Chamber has said in open court about it. I think we at that time said that we had read the correspondence and that at that point in time it was sufficient for us just the parties to be aware that the Chamber was informed about it but did not take any steps or did not take any decisions in respect of that. At that time, the Chamber considered the matter as a matter, rather, between the parties than involving the Chamber, although we very much appreciated to be informed about it. I think, then, that you never finally got an answer to your last letter. Is that where you say you insist on a certain response. I take it then that no other correspondence -- was there any more after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I must -- I must say, Your Honour, I didn't even have the courtesy of a response from Mrs. Del Ponte of any sort to my last letter, which is surprising, but by definition I haven't had any substantive response. It's just been ignored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the -- what do you expect the Chamber to do; to urge the Prosecution to respond to your last letter or what would you expect to be an appropriate reaction from the Chamber? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that seems, with respect, to be precisely the right question. We suggest that this is -- this is broadly speaking a matter within what I might call the overall supervisory responsibility of the Tribunal. The Prosecutor is -- and she has her own function, but she is an officer of this Tribunal, and Prosecution and Defence have their responsibilities to this Tribunal and, of course, widely to the community at large. We are very concerned that a statement of this sort has emanated, as it is quite clear it has, not from Mr. Harmon's team, but it is absolutely clear that it has come from within the Office of the Prosecution, and that is absolutely directly within Mrs. Del Ponte's responsibility. We do not believe -- I've made the qualifications in the letter because of course I don't have direct knowledge of the period from before last July, but as far as I'm aware, this unfortunate remark about Mr. Krajisnik having taken steps to delay his own trial while he, after all, has been in prison all that time, as far as we're aware is not correct. It was given currency in the media. It did come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you repeat the contents of the correspondence rather than answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do that for a deliberate reason, Your Honour, which is this is a public hearing, and I'm not stirring up trouble but I do wish it to be on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you'd say I'd rather first have the content of the correspondence on the record, please ask me and we'll decide whether we'll allow you to do that or not. But I did put a question to you. If you would prefer to have summarised the content of the correspondence, that's as such no problem, but you take your own course and you do not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am proposing to answer your question. It does require in this case just a little bit of introduction. I -- I wish -- I wish the issue to be plain publicly, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The answer to your question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in three lines; there has been a newspaper article in which the Office of the Prosecution is mentioned as the source of a critical remark, saying that Mr. Krajisnik did everything to delay the start of the proceedings. You checked that. Mr. Harmon denied that it came from his team, and you checked it with the -- with the journalist, and the journalist said it certainly came from the Office of the Prosecution, and you want this to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What I want, Your Honour, and I am in effect asking the Tribunal to express a firm view, which we then believe that Mrs. Del Ponte would conscientiously follow, that in relation to this particular contention which came from within the Office of the Prosecution, it should either be substantiated, and if Mrs. Del Ponte and the Office of the Prosecution are saying it is true, then it should be substantiated; and if it is substantiated, then I will graciously accept that it is correct. If it is not substantiated, then we believe it should be publicly withdrawn, because it is a grossly unfair thing to say if it is not true. It is grossly unfair for such a statement to have emanated from within the Office of the Prosecution - not from Mr. Harmon's team but from within the Office of the Prosecution - and then of course in the hands of a perfectly responsible journalist who is reporting what they can get from within the Office of the Prosecutor it's given media currency, and it is not fair on Mr. Krajisnik, and it should be corrected. So it's -- it should be -- it should be substantiated or it should be withdrawn, which is what I invited Mrs. Del Ponte to do, and her general response in relation to what she generally does in relation to media matters is not to the point, because her general response is not appropriately applicable to a situation where the specific contention has come from within her own office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. Any response at this moment or would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have a brief response. To make the record perfectly clear, in terms of the correspondence, not only did I immediately respond to Mr. Stewart, which he does not dispute, but Mrs. Del Ponte responded to Mr. Stewart as well, confirming that the position that I had taken in my letter to Mr. Stewart was essentially her position. Now, I find it very difficult to -- in a general sense, I don't deal with media matters, but I can imagine a public figure like Mrs. Del Ponte, who has matters reported in the media every day, some accurate, some inaccurate, having to respond to each assertion in the media. It would essentially consume and take her away from her job. Second of all, my recollection of the article that appeared in The Guardian was not a direct quote. It was a -- there was no attribution, of course, other than the general assertion that this information had come from an unknown source in the Office of the Prosecutor. My view, and I am not speaking other than my view, is that the matter should be laid to rest. It has been covered in Mrs. Del Ponte's response to Mr. Stewart when she adopted the position that I had taken in my correspondence with Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'd say that Ms. Del Ponte has taken the position that at least the statement as it appears in the Guardian is not a correct reflection of what the position of the OTP is, and you say if anything went wrong, let's not spend too much time on it - let's clearly establish this at this moment - and you'd rather insist on -- on, let's say, admitting that if it's wrong that it's a serious fault made by the Office of the Prosecution. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, not quite, Your Honour, because it is -- it is -- Mrs. Del Ponte has not taken the position -- and I'm quoting what Your Honour has just said. Your Honour said Mrs. Del Ponte has taken the position that at least the statement as it appears in The Guardian is not a correct reflection of what the position of the OTP is. That is not the position that Mrs. Del Ponte has taken at all. Mrs. Del Ponte has refused -- and we do strongly say, Your Honour, with respect, it's an abdication of her responsibility here. Mrs. Del Ponte has refused to take a position in relation to this. She has not denied the accuracy of -- of the report in the sense that it came from the Prosecution. The phrase used was "according to the Prosecution." Now, our starting points on that was when a -- after the first day of the trial, it was the following morning, when a journalist says "according to the Prosecution," the natural assumption is that it is talking about the Prosecution team in that case. Mr. Harmon did respond very quickly, I accept that entirely, and made it clear, and I accept that assurance unequivocally, that it was not Mr. Harmon's team. So that point had gone, but that meant that it did come from within Mrs. Del Ponte's office. She has refused to take a position on this. She has refused to say whether she is prepared to confirm what came from somebody under her aegis and within her responsibility and her office. She's refused to confirm it or withdraw it. And it is also -- though Mr. Harmon did respond very quickly to my letter, Mrs. Del Ponte did not respond at all quickly to my first letter and it is not satisfactory and it is in fact grossly discourteous. We don't take offence very easily but it is grossly discourteous for Mrs. Del Ponte simply to have ignored my last letter which set out a number of specific points in response to hers. We have work to do and we have time to do, and we are not impressed by the suggestion that Mrs. Del Ponte -- the implication is she's a busy woman and doesn't have time for all this. It was grossly discourteous of her not to have answered. But leaving that aside, the substance of the point is that this did come from the Prosecution, it has been reported, it is a very specific matter. If the Office of the Prosecution say it is correct, then they should substantiate it. If it is not correct, then they must withdraw it, and that is the only professional and responsible course. This is not a criticism in the least of the Prosecution team that we see in court here because it is absolutely clear this did not come from them, but up the chain to Mrs. Del Ponte as the person responsible for the person who was the source of this comment to the journalist, Mrs. Del Ponte must sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your position is clear. We'll consider what the role of the Chamber could be in this respect and whether we'll change our view or not or whether - which is also perhaps an option - whether the Chamber will express what in the view of the Chamber is true of -- what in the view of the Chamber would be -- whether the Chamber would take a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. position that it does not recognise what is stated in this article as being in accordance with what this Chamber considers to be their own experience. That might be a solution. I do not know whether the Chamber will urge the Prosecution, and of course that's also one of the issues, is whether it really has been said by someone in the Office of the Prosecutor. I mean, you have it confirmed by the journalist. It's not clearly denied. I would say it's more or less uninvestigated by the OTP. They say it's -- well, it would take a lot of work and we can't spend too much time on that. You disagree with that. That's clear. Whether -- whether the Chamber would take steps to clarify these issues is another matter, but we will consider it and we'll let you know. Having dealt with it -- having dealt with this issue -- well, having paid attention to this issue, which is a different matter, I now would like to further receive the evidence of Mr. Kirudja. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Harmon, in respect of the testimony of Mr. Kirudja, sometimes we go in details. If this Chamber sees a map with a lot of names of -- of states on it, then even without going through all the names of those states, the Chamber perfectly understands that these are troops sent by that state. This is just one example. Don't overestimate the intelligence of the Chamber, but it should not be underestimated either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, please be seated. I apologise that you had to wait for three-quarters of an hour. We had a late start because of logistical problems, and then we had a procedural issue which took some time as well, so therefore you had to wait and we feel sorry for you. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I'd like to focus your attention on some of the elements that are found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 120, your statement, paragraphs 64 through 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if Mr. Kirudja could be provided with a copy of Exhibit 120.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 64?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting at paragraph 64 going through paragraph 68. Let me summarise just to -- for a moment. These paragraphs recount a meeting between you and Danish military representatives had on the 26th of May with various individuals from Dvor, the mayor of Dvor, Mr. Borojevic, in which he made a request that 5.000 Muslims from Bosanski Novi wanted to transit through Sector North. In respect of that meeting, Mr. Kirudja, just tell us briefly, how did that meeting come about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is on 26th of May, as I recounted yesterday. Ours was a mandate in the United Nations Protected Areas in accordance with the objectives that I summarised from the Vance Plan. I was in Dvor, therefore, to advance those priorities and decided, of course, to get familiar not only with our own assets, meaning the police stations and the military deployed there, but also with local authorities. So as I was there my subject was not the one that is recounted in this paragraph. So suddenly my agenda is put aside and Mayor Borojevic begins to make the request that I summarised there. So I put down my agenda and start listening, and as I listen, something, what he's asking, struck me as terribly unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "I would like to have you assist in the transition of 5.000 people," not from his sector but from Bosanski Novi, which is on the other side of the international border. Now, what was strange, he wanted us to see to it that they are filmed as they transition the centre -- the UNPA, and that none of them remain in the UNPA, and that would be our responsibility according to his request. And finally, if I remember correctly, this as a demonstration, or words to the effect, to show our goodwill towards all these people as a humanitarian gesture on our part, so want the whole world to see that happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, what conclusion did you draw as to the viability of the international border that separated Bosnia from Croatia in the area of Dvor and Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, I wasn't really focused on the border itself. I was focused on what he was asking and the fact that the people were across the border, not the border itself, and the bizarre nature of the fact that he, the mayor of Dvor, is asking something on behalf of another jurisdiction and seeking to introduce it across the border, as you say, into our sector. And that struck me as a rather strange request to say the least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you later conclude anything about whether that was indeed a border, an international border that was respected by the people who lived in Sector North and the people who were in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the days went by, it was clear that that part of the international border where the Serbs controlled both sides was nothing more than a nominal border, and I mean from the opstina of Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Krupa, all the way in my sector - I'm thinking about the map I showed you yesterday - going westwards all the way to Bosanska Dubica. Both sides were controlled by Serbs, just roads and bridges between the two sides, and for Serb population, that was not really a border. Not so on the left side of that border on the opstina where the majority were Muslims, and I'm speaking about the opstina of Velika Kladusa as you go through to Bihac, that side. That was truly a border for whoever wanted to cross, but not so on that part of the border that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 66 of your written evidence, you state that the mayor commented that Bosanski Novi was now, and I'm quoting, "part of a new reality in the form of the Serbian Republic of BiH." Can you comment on that further?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary of the sequence of the conversation that I'd begun in an attempt to understand why the mayor of Dvor would be asking to undertake this massive transit of people. Our series of questions that I asked and culminating to this statement, why would be -- why would you, the mayor of Dvor, be talking to me or relaying to me something that is being ascribed to the mayor or the authorities in Bosanski Novi - both of you are Serbs - about the aspirations of Muslims? And I remember specifically saying I always understood you when you speak very passionately about the aspirations of Serbs, but these are Muslims whom you told me are leaving voluntarily and want to cross over here. Why would people be leaving voluntarily if everything is as peaceful across the border as you suggest in this what you call magnanimous effort of the Serbs to show their humanitarian concern? Why would they be leaving? And the answer was, well -- words to the effect that Bosanski Novi was now part of a new reality. But before we even got into that, I remember where we were meeting was just a few metres away, in a conference room, to his office. I remember him rushing to the office and saying, "If you don't believe me," he made a telephone call, and he said, "Here is the mayor. Would you come and talk to him." At that moment I wasn't quite ready to do that and I declined to him, to hear this new reality. He began to see my questions were something is not quite understandable about what you're telling me. So when he mentioned that reality in the context of saying he will explain to you, the other mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your statement in paragraph 64 to 68 is quite detailed. I won't ask you any more questions about that particular meeting. The Judges may have some questions for you, Mr. Kirudja, or Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But if I could have Mr. Kirudja shown the next exhibit, which will be Exhibit 126. Is that correct? 120 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P125.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Exhibit 125. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you inspect that briefly without making any comment on it, Mr. Kirudja, please. Mr. Kirudja, examining this particular exhibit, 125, did you prepare this exhibit and do you see your signature at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is in my handwriting and as well as signed by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I see at the end of your name another acronym, CAC, which we'll be seeing again. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my title, Civil Affairs Coordinator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to direct your attention to the three lines from the bottom of the first page, which I will read: "Would appreciate if UNHCR could assist in obtaining accurate and firsthand information on the story," and the story being 5.000 Muslims who were allegedly leaving Bosanski Novi voluntarily. Why did you request that UNHCR receive accurate information about this story?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, a little -- this is in the context of what I discussed yesterday about the various responsibilities in a complex mission such as the UN involving various elements. I reported to the director of civil affairs. At the end of that second page, you will see it's to the DCA, UNPROFOR, Director of Civil Affairs. We were mandated to have responsibility within the UN protected area. This matter, as you can see for yourselves clearly, is about refugees outside the border of the UNPA. Once the matter is brought to my attention, I couldn't put to bear any resources under UNPROFOR to operate across the border to ascertain what I am hearing, because we have no mandate. All the resources that we have are defined within the UNPA, and the matter is about possible refugees in Bosanski Novi wanting to transit in the sector. The only agency that would have the mandate to go there and see for themselves would have been UNHCR. So the intent and purpose of this memorandum is to now prepare the ground for me to have people who will have legitimacy to go across and take a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention now to the second page of this document, Mr. Kirudja. The -- starting at the second line from the top, let me read the last sentence: "We have indications that this story may have other political ramifications." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall, the mayor is saying bring the ICRC and the UNPROFOR to film these people transiting through the sector on condition they do not stay in the sector. The only way they could come out would be across the confrontation line to the other side controlled by the Croatian authorities at the end -- at the north, meaning there are two corridors of roads that exited through this sector, one corridor through Vojnic and out into Karlovac, the other corridor through Glina and out into Sisak. The political ramification is that these people will be moving from an international jurisdiction in Bosnia through the UN zone, UNPA, into Croatian territory. There -- the political implications of all of that are inescapable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, let me direct your attention to the next exhibit. This would be Exhibit 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this Exhibit relates to the contents of paragraphs 69 through 76 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 120 --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 69 through 76 of your written evidence, Mr. Kirudja, and I will summarise very briefly those paragraphs that deal -- in fact, they exhaustively recount a meeting that took place on the following day in Tapusko on the 27th of May, and in that meeting the mayor from Bosanski Novi, Radomir Pasic, attended with his delegation, and he came unannounced and tried to convince you to allow 5.000 Muslims from Bosanski Novi to transit through your jurisdiction. So that's a summary of what's found in those paragraphs, but, Mr. Kirudja, do you have in front of you the next exhibit, which will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 125?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that number, but there's something on my monitor which is a memorandum that I recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last exhibit was P125.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it that this will then be P126.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, will you inspect Prosecutor's Exhibit P126 before I ask you some questions about it. Mr. Kirudja, the first page of this exhibit, on the top it says "UNPROFOR Message Form." Do you recognise this exhibit and do your initials appear on it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is in my handwriting and is initialed by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting on the next page, the document with the caption "Fax Transmission," at the bottom of which it says: "Sincerely," the handwriting is -- if I interpret the handwriting here, it says Jens Brosted. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning the page one more page, starting at the top it says: "Jens Brosted report on meeting regarding Muslim inhabitants of Bosanski Novi at headquarters UNPA north on May 28, 1992." Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While I'm on that caption that I just read, it says that the meeting took place on May 28, 1992. Is that correct or is that an error?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My note -- my diary seems to indicate it was on 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Kirudja, who is Jens Brosted?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jens Brosted was the officer who UNHCR supplied at my request to be based at the headquarters, at our headquarters in Tapusko quite early, not because -- long before or, rather, before the meeting in Dvor the mandate of the mission included, and we anticipated it would include a lot about refugees, and since we were to prepare for their voluntary return, I went to Zagreb and made an appeal urgently that they collocate one of their staffers in my office, and Jens Brosted was one of the first they sent to my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could turn to your written evidence, Prosecutor's Exhibit 120, and refer you to paragraph 70 in that document. And again I won't go into great detail about this meeting because it's very exhaustively covered, but I want to focus your attention on the following: In paragraph 70, first you say: "I asked why a human being would want to leave the safety of his or her house if everything was as peaceful and orderly as portrayed. Pasic responded: 'I admit that the Muslims have been under pressure from armed Serbian irregulars,' implying that the regular forces of law and order had nothing to do with the harassment of Muslims with a view to force them to evacuate." Now, did he explain to you who those Serb irregulars were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was -- he mentioned that, as this paragraph hints, because this was again a three-hour meeting where he repeated almost verbatim the elements of the earlier demarche that was put to me by Mr. Jugo Borojevic in Dvor, again, basically to leave voluntarily, we have a new reality around, and all of that. All of those were repeated almost verbatim. And I started now asking him - because something was counter-intuitive in what they were telling me - how would these people -- aren't they in their home? Yes. So he explained to me this new reality, what they had decided in the meetings, deadlines for when they're supposed to -- I mean the Muslims are supposed to disarm and swear allegiance to this new reality, and he went on and on. And then I said to him, still I don't know how a human being can voluntarily leave the safety of their home if all is peaceful and you are doing this magnanimous thing, humanitarian thing, why are they leaving? Looks to me like somebody -- is it you? Who is this? trying -- or why are they trying to get away from their homes? In order to forestall the implication of my question, he said, oh, well, some Serbian irregulars. Remember his chief of police is also there in the meeting. Everybody is there. They couldn't just as well say, We are the ones forcing -- we are forcing them out. No. Some irregulars. That was the context in which he explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me direct -- and I take it you didn't believe him.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct you to paragraph 71. At the end of that paragraph on page 18, there is a reference to -- I will quote you, quote the statement: "Rather, it became eventually clearer that they were being forced out of Bosanski Novi because they had first refused to sign allegiance to a newly created Serb Republic of BiH, and that this was later compounded by their refusal to relinquish whatever weapons they had for self-defence to the Serbs." Now, what was the significance to you of the fact that the people who were going to be evacuated through your sector had refused to sign an oath of allegiance to the newly created Serb Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of the language you see in this paragraph is not a language coming from me. It's a summary of a language coming from the delegation itself. Fact: That they had refused to sign allegiance. That's not my language. That's Mr. Pasic explaining to me, because the incredulity I showed earlier, the elements that ended up proving to me there was nothing voluntary. So at that moment he is explaining me the refusal to disarm, the fact that therefore there were irregular police, all of those are explanations coming directly. I'm summarising that explanation. The only conclusion I'm making, that did not come from Mr. Pasic and indeed did not sit well with him, is the fact that this does not seem voluntary then on the one side. I told him, this -- in that sense they're not leaving because it's a voluntary thing. Okay, he says, I admit. All right. The next thing, if he explains me, well, they also did not want to sign allegiance and fight and sign the allegiance to this new reality called Serbian Republic of BiH, then he explains to me they had a period between 6th and 8th of May with a deadline of 9th of May where they're supposed to disarm. He explains to me actually they did not, and I recall him saying they brought a bunch of bags inside which there were wooden rifles and spent shells. They didn't disarm. But they won't fight, he tells me, for Izetbegovic government or our ours. And I said, if they are not going to disarm, they are not going to fight, again there is something counter-intuitive. Why would people not disarm and won't fight for somebody else? The only conclusion I could draw there is they needed this for self-defence. That he didn't say. That is the conclusion I'm saying. If they won't give up their weapons, if they won't fight, then the only other thing left is that they kept those weapons for their self-defence, and that caused the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer you to Mr. Brosted's report, the last page of it. At the bottom it's marked 5/5. And in this report, Mr. Brosted reports about this meeting, and he says -- and I'm reading from the second complete paragraph down. It says: "Major stumbling blocks were stated to be that UNHCR seeks to assist and protect refugees and displaced persons, not to create refugees."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Show me again the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in Mr. Brosted's report, the exhibit that's before you. It's on the last page.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second complete paragraph down, there's some -- the paragraph starts, "I informed of the --"

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you go down, the fifth line, I'm quoting from the fifth line: "Major stumbling blocks were stated to be that UNHCR seeks to assist and protect refugees and displaced persons, not to create refugees, that the Vance Plan was based on the basic principle that the ethnic composition of communities should not be altered." Now, focusing on that element of the meeting, which I understand was the message that was conveyed to Mayor Pasic and his delegation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and by me, not by Jens Brosted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What was the reaction of the Bosnian Serb delegation to that information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made clear when I had heard all the explanations to my questions, and I told Mr. Pasic, one, we are now clear that you are attempting to move 5.000 people out of their own homes involuntarily. We, as the UN, cannot and absolutely could not be party to making refugees out of people in their own homes. I made that clear to him. It is also contrary to our mandate, as I explained yesterday. We were supposed to, under the Vance Plan, to act in such a way that the situation becomes conducive to people who had already left to return, not to cause new ones to leave, which is the reference to that part of the Vance Plan. When he heard me on that, he had no doubt about it, and he looked at me and said, "It's clear that you're not being cooperative. Who is your boss so we can go to him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer you to one more line, and that is on the same page, six lines up. I'm going to quote -- six lines up from the bottom, and I will quote part of that sentence. It says: "CAC was blunt in saying that we should stop pretending that the persons were leaving voluntarily." Is that when Mr. Pasic or other members of his delegation said to you that you essentially were not being cooperative?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. At that point -- these meetings are very polite. I want to be clear that we were not really shouting or complaining. I would -- much of all this I'm busy listening to him. This meeting was more than three hours. When he kept repeating over and over things that I had heard, that's when I said, Mr. Mayor, I've heard you. You can stop now. It's clear they're not moving voluntarily by your own admission. That's what it means. So he doesn't keep on repeating over and over things that he had already mentioned for which we asked questions, for which he supplied answers and for which we are drawing the conclusion. They are not there for leaving voluntarily, Mr. Mayor. He said, Yes, I admit. Then let's be clear on that. Don't tell me they're leaving voluntarily Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any more. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with that particular exhibit. If we could go to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's -- will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 127. This, Mr. Kirudja, is an exhibit that was directed to you. The date that appears on this is the 5th of June, 1992. It is from Mr. Brosted, and the subject is 5.000 Muslims from Bosanski Novi. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for the Court's and your information, we will be presenting an exhibit that you actually received this report on the 9th of June. That will be a subsequent exhibit, but I just wanted to focus on this because of what earlier you had requested in an earlier exhibit, that is, trying to find out independent verification of the story. And so let me -- this is -- to summarise this exhibit, this is an exhibit from Mr. Brosted recounting reports of interviews of two Bosnian Muslims from Bosanski Novi who had been interviewed in Zagreb. And let me -- is it clear, then, that this document -- first of all, Mr. Kirudja, is Mr. Brosted attempting to develop that independent information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read part of this document. I will read it starting at page 3 -- I'm sorry, starting at paragraph number 3 on the first page: "CH confirmed that disarmament of Muslim villages had taken place. He was in the village of Suhaca and had been the first one -- and had been the first one to lay down arms. When they had done that, some Serbian territorial military moved in together with Krajina police and told them to leave the houses. The houses were searched while they -- while the villagers waited in the field for five to six hours. After the search, they were allowed back and told they would be all right. However, a few days after the first shelling started, a grenade landed in his yard. Shelling was by cannons and mortars from neighbouring Serb villages." "4. The informant did not know of any agreement on disarmament, had not been involved nor had he knowledge of any symbolic denouncement of an agreement. He noted that no Serb had been killed in this area. Serbian villages had not been disarmed, rather, helicopters had come in with supplies from Banja Luka and Knin. "5. On 23 May 1992, the villages of Donji Agici, Gornji Agici and Hozici was burned. On Sunday, 24 May, a big convoy was formed from six villages. Peoples felt compelled to flee because their villages were destroyed. In his village, Suhaca, the fires had been started on the edges of the village to frighten people out. CH had also seen Hozici on fire. He had heard reports on destruction of other villages and believed the process to be going on. "6. The convoy had formed in two groups, and he did not know how far the first one had gone. The main convoy was stopped in Blagaj by persons in Serbian military uniforms (just like JNA) and Serb paramilitary groups. From symbols on their uniform, it was deduced that they should be under the control of the Serbian Democratic Party and Mayor Pajic. The Serbs at Blagaj had wanted to mobilise both men and women. Supposedly the convoy had also been promised free passage in order to 'clean' the area." Now, just focusing on those paragraphs, Mr. Kirudja, did this report that you received later on the 9th of May shed more light as to what was happening in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, and as you can see, it is addressed to me from Mr. Jens Brosted so that we can begin to corroborate the conclusions we were making based on what the Serb authorities were telling us themselves; that these refugees were already moving and -- voluntarily, and we didn't believe it. We wanted now to see whether our belief, based on his own explanation, would be corroborated, and this does so, that they are really not voluntary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to paragraph 8 in this exhibit, and I will read it: "I mentioned the two names given to us as spokespersons for the group," and then there is report 29/5/92. Paragraph -- I have gone through that. It looks like paragraph 9: "They were believed to be imprisoned or kept with the men as 'hostages' in a school in Blagaj." Now, the two names that were given to you earlier, if you take a look at the earlier report by Mr. Brosted in paragraph 9, were Sifet Barjaktarevic and Fikret Hamzagic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by earlier report by Brosted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the previous exhibit, 126, the report that --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any previous exhibits. I always keep the current.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that could be returned to you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would just refer to the previous exhibit, at paragraph 9 of Mr. Brosted's report. It appears on page 5/5. Two names are Sifet Barjaktarevic and Fikret Hamzagic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These names were already in my own notes and they were already also in paragraph 70 of my own testimony, and they were given to us by Pasic himself, that these are the people we could talk to to affirm that the Muslims were leaving voluntarily. That's in what context they were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the report Prosecutor's Exhibit 127, which is before you, the report from Mr. Brosted of the interview of these two people, in paragraph 8 refers to those two men who are believed to be essentially hostages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I've finished with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do we break, Mr. President, at 10.30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although we started a bit later. We have two breaks, but usually we have to stop after one hour and a half, and since we started late, if you'd say this is a suitable moment, we'll have the break now. If you say I'd like to use the next ten minutes, that's fine as well. But somewhere within the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is suitable -- actually, I can carry on with the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the next exhibit could be given to Mr. Kirudja. Prosecutor's Exhibit 128.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, this is an exhibit that is dated 6th of June, 1992, from C. Thornberry, Director of Civil Affairs UNPROFOR Belgrade, directed to your attention, the subject of which is the 5 June sitrep. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read this paragraph to you: "Please investigate immediately and in coordination with CIVPOL and advise urgently on the following: 5 June sitrep indicates that one of Dan patrols --" that refers to the Danish patrols; is that correct, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... observed 100 women and children being brought into stadium with their heads covered with cloths and carrying plastic bags with ten armed persons guarding stadium. CIVPOL here will be giving instructions to their personnel." Signed by Cedric Thornberry. Do you recognise Mr. Thornberry's signature?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Cedric Thornberry, first of all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's my boss. He's the director of civil affairs. And this is the first indication to me that this whole matter of which I was seized on the ground is beginning to attract his attention too because he's seated in Belgrade. Important: That is where our headquarters had begun to resort after Sarajevo became untenable. We began now to go back to Belgrade. He's seated in Belgrade and reading these situation reports, he begins now to -- at me -- his attention begins to be seized of the matter, and he is saying to me to give him further -- investigate and appraise him fuller on this matter. And as you can see on the left corner of that exhibit, I now pass this to the chief of -- chief of police in my sector so that the civil police unit could begin now, whereever they are located, the process of doing the kind of investigation that would result in the information I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this -- what you've told us earlier, that the civilian -- the CIVPOL chief of police could not go into Bosnia to do an investigation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is the dilemma and why, when you work in a bureaucracy, some of these things look strange. They are dancing around this idea that what you want to do -- get, you have to get it without doing it. And there he's saying go investigate, but don't go where you have no mandate, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes -- that's a good time to conclude because the next exhibit will be the response of Mr. Kirudja to this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then adjourn until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, perhaps the Chamber would like to say a few words again on the procedural issue, not to start a new debate on it, but not necessarily now. If either at the end of this portion of the hearing or the next one Mr. Tieger could come, or if you would relay whatever we say about it to Mr. Tieger, I leave it up to you. Whether you want to call him at a later stage or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll get Mr. Tieger here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, at a time, not necessarily now. Then there was another issue that was about correspondence. I'd like to say the following, and that would then also be, as far as the Chamber is concerned, the last word spoken about the issue, at least as it stands now. The matter has been explained and is publicly put on record. The Chamber expresses itself in the following way: Whatever may have caused the delay of the start of the trial for reasons in the past, the Chamber has not experienced any effort by the Defence -- and I am now concentrating on since last July, the present Defence team. The Chamber has not experienced any effort by the Defence to delay the start of the trial inconsistent with professional responsibilities and duties of counsel and therefore it does not recognise as reflecting reality what is said in this newspaper article. Then, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very, very difficult for me in this situation because Tribunal has said it's the last word, and of course in the end, if I'm told that I simply cannot say another word, I have to respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you know -- you know the Latin expression nitus finiri aparta, which means at a certain moment you have to end a discussion. The Chamber has established that the Defence does not blame this Prosecution team and seems to have a -- well, a dispute with The Prosecutor which does not affect - and that's clear, I think, from the wording of what I just said - does not affect this Trial Chamber or these proceedings but is mainly about, well, an impression given to the outside world. This Chamber clearly now has stated that whatever has appeared in that newspaper article is not something the Chamber has experienced since July of last year. On the contrary. And of course the wording has been chosen carefully, not under all circumstances a search for the delay of the proceedings is unprofessional or would be inconsistent with duties of counsel. I have asked in my past very often, for very good reasons, you can think about the Tadic case, to have the start of trial put at a moment which was considered to be most appropriate in view of the Defence. There's nothing unprofessional. There's nothing wrong with that. What is in the newspaper article, however, is of a totally different nature, and the Chamber has clearly expressed that it has not experienced any effort in that sense by the Defence team. And if there is any further thing to be said about it, the Chamber would receive written submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take that opportunity, because I will write to the Chamber to make it clear that I'm afraid that, although I appreciate the helpfulness, that what the Trial Chamber has said does simply not deal with the substantial fundamental point of our statement. I will put that in writing to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I do understand that. Of course the Trial Chamber has considered also what is within its competence, and I don't know whether a judgement on the behaviour on publicity of Ms. Del Ponte would automatically be within the competence of this Trial Chamber. Whatever you'd like to add to it, please write it down --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- submit it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not promising you will get -- if you ask for decisions you will get them, but you will certainly get a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I know -- I know I will get the courtesy of a response from the Tribunal. I'm absolutely confident about that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll now continue the examination of Mr. Kirudja. Mr. Kirudja, I apologise for you having to listen to procedural issues rather than anything else. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we left before the break with Prosecutor's 128, which was a memo from Cedric Thornberry to you, dated the 6th of June. If I could turn to the next exhibit, which will be the Prosecutor's Exhibit 129. Mr. Kirudja, this Prosecutor's Exhibit 129 is an UNPROFOR message form dated the 8th of June, 1992. It appears to bear your initials and it is accompanied by a memorandum dated the 8th of June, 1992, the subject of which is "Investigative report on the displaced people observed in Bosanski Novi." At the end it also has your name typewritten and appears to bear your initials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this, Mr. Kirudja, your response to Mr. Thornberry's inquiry to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- investigate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just draw your attention to a part of this memorandum which appears, in most parts, to summarise previous communications that you had sent up your chain of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the memorandum, the last paragraph in the memorandum, which I will read: "On 27 May, the mayor of Bosanski Novi came to see the CAC in Tapusko on his own initiative. With him was a member of his Executive Committee, Mr. Rade Palije. The UNHCR representative Mr. Jens Brosted joined the meeting at the invitation of the CAC. From that meeting we concluded that the mayor had collaborators in the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina,' and was acting on their behalf or interest." Can you comment to us about that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an internal memorandum within an organisation that jealously guards mandates and jealously does not want to see a cross between areas of responsibility or stepping outside of that. A lot of this memo is trying to put things clear with that regard. It is also a response from the next reporting level where I'm getting an instruction to investigate something that I have been already informing them. And of course you don't tell your boss you didn't read what you said. So I have to bring together. This is nothing new, and it's been done within the terms of our reference. So this paragraph is talking from the point of view of our mandate in the -- in the UNPA. The mayor being referred to is the mayor of Dvor, not the mayor of Bosanski Novi. It's the mayor of Dvor. We have business with the mayor of Dvor. I have mandate with the mayor of Dvor. I have, therefore, to tell my boss it started with the mayor of Dvor in the course of our business, and he seems to have "collaboration" with the mayor across. That's the reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I've concluded with that exhibit. If we could go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, sir, the -- where it says, "The mayor had collaborators," there you did not refer to the mayor of Bosanski Novi who came to see you but the mayor of Dvor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because that's what I'm telling my boss, otherwise he will say, What is your business with the mayor of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This exhibit, Your Honours, relates to paragraph 77 of the written evidence of Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, would you inspect Prosecutor's Exhibit 130. It is an UNPROFOR message form dated the 6th of June from civil affairs officer Sector North. It bears a name P. Raffone at the bottom, and then accompanying this exhibit is a memorandum dated the 6th of June, subject "Potential Muslim refugees in BH," at the end of which is the name Paolo Raffone, Civil Affairs Officer, and at the bottom of which it says "Released by Charles Kirudja," and that appears to be your initials over your typewritten name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're familiar with both of these documents then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start off by identifying who is Mr. Raffone, and what role did he have in your office?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's one of a number of civil affairs officers reporting directly to me who would be on a day-to-day task on the various parts of our mandate, and then he would first pursue that part, make a report as necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were -- what were his actual responsibilities and duties in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had tasked him to look at the side of our mandate that deals with refugees and displaced persons, overall mandate, of course, being what I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this -- to summarise the memorandum, this memorandum relates a phone conversation that Mr. Raffone had with the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I take a look at the second paragraph on the memorandum -- let me just read the -- let me read the first two paragraphs. "On 1 June 1992, the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Kupresanin, called the civil affairs office in Sector North. He conveyed some information concerning the Muslim refugees' flow that might originate from his area towards Croatia passing through the crossing points in Dvor and Karlovac. The mayor's information can be summarised as follows: "The mayors of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most, and the one in Banja Luka had contacts about the situation of the Muslim population in the area." And it goes on, and four paragraphs below where I just ended reading, I'll pick up. It says: "The mayor estimates that some 15.000 persons have already left their normal place of residence, moving towards Dvor, and some more 15.000 might follow in a short time." Now, what, Mr. Kirudja, is the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's significant pretty much at the first line of this document. This is a telephone call he received while in the day-to-day course in the office. It is dated June. The first meeting about these refugees was on 26th of May. In short, we had become seized of this matter, and because of his alertness to it, while a lesser competent officer would have just spoken on the telephone and forgotten all about it, he realised the importance and took notes about it and recorded precisely what the mayor, Kupresanin, was saying. And he is -- the two elements that we wanted to highlight was this matter is continuing and is gathering momentum. It is not just Bosanski Novi, it spans an area larger, and it is the second paragraph that will give you that impression of the area that this matter spans. Secondly, the numbers we could expect are not just the 5.000 that we started talking about. It's being telegraphed to us that this number could grow three or four times, to start with, and then double, potentially, with another 15.000. That coming from the telephone was the significance of this matter, that we needed to be vigilant about what's going on on this, and it is all headed our way in the United Nations protected area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, given your previous contact with the mayor of Bosanski Novi, did you have concern as to why the potentially 30.000 Muslims in the municipalities that are named in the second paragraph might be leaving their homes and coming your way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, we are now beginning to watch out to understand what's going on. The only evidence we had up to this point was the explanation from the authorities from Bosanski Novi. Nothing would have told us to expand that understanding beyond the area he was explaining us, that is Bosanski Novi and the villages that he named in his presentation, particularly Blagaj. The second information we had to confirm our understanding of that reality came from Mr. Brosted debriefing those two people we had. But I repeat, at this moment we really don't have a full picture, nor do we have a conclusion about what is happening in all these areas. It only meant we are now vigilant, we're trying to understand who, what, and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you proceeded to make an effort, you and members of your staff proceeded to make an effort to refine your knowledge of --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And understanding. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this particular -- I take it this particular memorandum was then sent up to the civil affairs officer in Sector North, and this was forwarded up your chain of command further.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is actually addressed to my director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to the prospect of 30.000 Muslims from those municipalities transiting through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did note in the first message on one of the exhibits here I had signalled to my headquarters this is not just a humanitarian problem. It has the potential for a lot of political problems to be caused by 30.000 people trying to transit. Remember, they were not even supposed to stay there, to transit from one jurisdiction, transit through another, headed to a third one. The complications that would occur if I don't alert them, it would be the first question to me as an official there, why didn't you alert us to this potentiality? And that is what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the next exhibit, which is also the 6th of June, the same day as Exhibit 130. This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 131. Mr. Kirudja, this exhibit is two pages. The first page is an UNPROFOR message form. It is dated the 6th of June from Civil Affairs Sector North to UNPROFOR in Belgrade and UNHCR in Zagreb. It has your name at the bottom and appears to have your initials at the bottom of the page. And the next page of this exhibit is a memorandum dated the 6th of June, subject "Displaced persons from Bosanski Novi referred to in yesterday's military sitrep," and it has your typewritten name at the bottom. Do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me refer to the second page of this document, and let me read from the first full paragraphs underneath the caption, starting at the top: "The duty officer at DANCON/HQ in Kostajnica informed the CAC --" that's you, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... over the telephone that at 1900 hours sitrep will report as follows about the 350 displaced persons reported to have been gathered in a football field in Bosanski Novi. The 350 persons were seen to be loaded onto buses to unknown destinations in Bosnia. They are no longer at the football stadium. DANCON had no knowledge of who was loading the persons into buses. At no time did they cross River Una into the UNPA, i.e., into Dvor or the surrounding area." Now, Mr. Kirudja, in this -- first of all, what was the significance of this information to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, we are now rapidly seeing the ramifications of refugees in bigger numbers being noted and causing a response from the various units of this mission with various parts. This mission has military, police, and NGO. A military officer of this contingent now notices that, and it's about refugees, and the only person he can try to get sense from is me, because this is not a military matter, so he gives me a call and warns me we are going to report this. The military didn't know about our meeting with the passage or whatever. So we are seeing now the various parts of this mission beginning to see the various ramifications of what's about to happen. And I was grateful for his call, because when these reports go up various channels, they trigger different reactions at the headquarters in Zagreb. So I am trying now to close the understanding by sending a comment, knowing that when they meet in the morning -- the ritual is that every headquarters has what we call meeting where they look at all the information for the day and plan their day. If they see the report that 350 people are gathered in a football field, my director will say, "Ah, what is my person saying about it over there and why isn't he telling me about it?" So this report is to try to close that understanding and tell them, look, we may be in the UNPA, our mandate may be limited to the UNPA, but things are happening across the border that have significant impact, and that's what the significance of this memo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit relates to paragraphs 82 and 83 of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And quoting from paragraph 83 of your written evidence, Mr. Kirudja, this says that it was the --: "It was, however, the first time that a collection of a large number of people had been detected by DANCON's reconnaissance," and that paragraph ends by saying, "This was the first time they had seen for themselves what appeared to be concrete evidence of a mass roundup of people." Now, at the same time you received this report on June the 6th, were refugees coming -- Muslim refugees and non-Serb refugees coming across the border in small lots and groups?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those people being debriefed by members of your staff or by NGOs who were operating in your theatre of operations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this report from DANCON and the reports that you were receiving from the NGOs of interviews of refugee -- non-Serb refugees who were coming into Sector North help clarify in your mind what was happening in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in slow steps. We were not rushing to judgement; we were open-minded. But we were beginning slowly to comprehend. At this point in June, the full picture wasn't really clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I've concluded with that exhibit, Mr. Kirudja. We'll go to the next exhibit. This exhibit is 137?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P132.
